summary: Describes how to express media transport over TCP using the Session Description Protocol. It defines the SDP TCP protocol identifier, a setup attribute describing how the connection is established, and a connection attribute for re-establishing a dropped connection. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Before a video call starts, both sides share a note about how they will talk. This memo adds to that note the option to use a steady, reliable line, and says who dials whom.

questions: what is the sdp setup attribute
how does sdp describe tcp media
sdp actpass vs active vs passive
subtitle: How an SDP session description says that media flows over TCP, and who dials whom.

tldr.problem: SDP could only describe unreliable, connectionless media over RTP/AVP and UDP, but some applications are better served by TCP, which needs a decision about which side opens the connection and when.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a 'TCP' protocol identifier for the 'm' line, a 'setup' attribute (active, passive, actpass, holdconn) that says who initiates the connection, and a 'connection' attribute (new or existing) that says whether to keep or replace the current TCP connection.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can negotiate TCP-based media with the offer/answer model and can reuse or re-establish connections cleanly. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4572.

facts.label: Port on an active endpoint's m line
Default setup
facts.value: active in offer, passive in answer

today: RFC 4145 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 4572. Read the two together when working with TCP-based media in SDP.

sections.title: Why SDP Needed TCP
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (RFC 2327) is a textual format for describing a multimedia session. It does not define a protocol of its own, and descriptions can be carried over many existing protocols such as SIP, RTSP, HTTP or email.

SDP defined only two protocol identifiers, RTP/AVP and UDP, both unreliable and connectionless. That suits many media streams, but some applications are better off with TCP. TCP raises two questions that UDP does not: how and when should the endpoints set up the connection?

RFC 4145 answers with one new protocol identifier, TCP, and two new attributes, setup and connection.
sections.eli5: Before this memo, the note could only describe sending media like tossing postcards. Now it can also describe a phone line that stays open, and a phone line needs someone to dial first.

sections.title: The TCP Protocol Identifier
sections.content:
An SDP media description starts with an m= line that has a proto field. This RFC defines a new value for that field: TCP.

Like the UDP identifier, TCP describes only the transport and not the upper-layer protocol. An m line that uses it MUST also name the application-layer protocol with an fmt identifier. The media is then carried using TCP.
sections.eli5: The word TCP on the line says which kind of road to use. You still have to say what kind of vehicle is driving on it.

sections.title: The Setup Attribute
sections.content:
The setup attribute says which endpoint should initiate the TCP connection, that is, send the first SYN. It can be a session-level or a media-level attribute and has four values:

  • active: the endpoint will initiate an outgoing connection.
  • passive: the endpoint will accept an incoming connection.
  • actpass: the endpoint can either accept or initiate.
  • holdconn: the endpoint does not want the connection established for the time being.

The value is negotiated with the offer/answer model of RFC 3264. The offerer states the roles it is willing to play, and the answerer picks the roles both sides will actually perform. The default is active in the offer and passive in the answer.

The active endpoint SHOULD connect to the port number on the other side's m line. Its own port number is irrelevant, so an active endpoint SHOULD put port 9 (the discard port) there. A port of zero is allowed only to mark an m line that is or has been refused.
sections.eli5: It is like deciding who will phone whom. One side says 'you call me', 'I will call you', 'either way is fine', or 'not yet', and the other side picks an answer that fits.

sections.title: The Connection Attribute
sections.content:
SDP can be exchanged again after a session has started, for example to change media parameters or redirect media. A later exchange could mean 'keep the current TCP connection' or 'make a new one'. The media-level connection attribute removes that doubt. It has two values, new and existing.

An offerer that wants to keep using the current connection MUST say existing. One that wants a fresh connection MUST say new. An initial offer, or an offer that changes the IP address or port of an m line, uses new. The value in the answer is the result. If the offer says new, the answer MUST say new. If the offer says existing, the answer may say existing or new.

When the result is existing, the ports, addresses and setup values from the exchange are ignored. An offerer that sends existing with passive must be ready for a new connection in case the answer says new. To avoid holding resources, it may send holdconn instead, but then a further offer/answer exchange is needed if the answerer picks new. The default value is new in both offers and answers.
sections.eli5: When the two sides talk again, this says 'keep using the same phone line' or 'hang up and dial a fresh one'.

sections.title: Connection Management
sections.content:
An endpoint that is supposed to initiate a new connection SHOULD do so as soon as it can, even if it will not send media right away, so that the remote side can send media. Some endpoints must wait first, for example a wireless terminal that has to set up a radio bearer.

If an endpoint finds that the TCP connection for an m line has closed and should be restored, it SHOULD run a new offer/answer exchange with connection set to new. When a result of new is agreed, the endpoints SHOULD close any previous connection that is still up as soon as the exchange completes, and the application must keep data in sync across the two connections.

Endpoints typically keep the connection until the session expires, is ended, or a new connection value is given. The SDP direction attribute (such as a=sendonly) affects the media sent, not the TCP connection itself. Individual applications may add rules for graceful termination.
sections.eli5: Whoever is supposed to dial should do it right away, even if they have nothing to say yet, so the other side can talk. If the line drops, they agree to dial again.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four examples, all for a T.38 fax session. In the first, the offerer at 192.0.2.2 says passive on port 54111. The answerer at 192.0.2.1 says active with port 9, then connects to port 54111.

In the second, the offerer says actpass and the answerer replies passive on port 54321, so the offerer makes the connection. In the third, the answerer reuses that connection with existing, and the other side answers active with port 9 because it is the one that originally connected.

In the fourth, an offer asks to reuse the connection, but the answerer, now a different endpoint at 192.0.2.3, does not know the old connection. It answers active and new, connects to port 54111, and the old connection is closed. The offerer used passive rather than holdconn, which saved a second offer/answer round.
sections.eli5: The examples show different ways two fax machines could agree on who dials, and what happens when one of them does not remember the old line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: An attacker who can change the connection and setup values could make endpoints rebuild connections for no reason or stop them from connecting at all. The RFC therefore strongly RECOMMENDS integrity protection for the session descriptions. For SDP carried in SIP, S/MIME is described as the natural choice for end-to-end integrity, and other applications MAY use another form of integrity protection. General SDP security issues are left to RFC 2327.
sections.eli5: If a trickster could change the note, they could make the two sides keep hanging up or never connect, so the note should be sealed so changes can be noticed.

viz.caption: ALLOWED SETUP ANSWERS FOR EACH OFFER

data.title: Passive offer, active answer
data.code:
Offer:
m=image 54111 TCP t38
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.2
a=setup:passive
a=connection:new

Answer:
m=image 9 TCP t38
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.1
a=setup:active
a=connection:new
